extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime/current world events (WWII-era)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing or assembling a wire-service wartime newspaper article: include dateline/byline, summarize main developments up front, and support with sourced dispatches, eyewitness detail, official communiqués, and theater-by-theater accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and delay labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dateline with location and date and indicate when dispatches are delayed (e.g., "NORTH AFRICA, Feb. 3 (Delayed).").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the dateline at the top of the dispatch to show where the report originates and whether it is a delayed or immediate dispatch; this communicates timeliness and geographic context to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byline and correspondent identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the reporter and their role or affiliation (e.g., "By WILLIAM KING, United Press War Correspondent", "By JAMES ... for the Associated Press").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the correspondent's name and affiliation (wire service or organization) and, when relevant, their position (war correspondent) or location to establish authority and provenance of firsthand reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and wire-service attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute information to its source or wire service (examples: "By the Associated Press", "describes the following dispatch written for the Associated Press").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state when material is from a wire service, another correspondent, or official communiqués; attribute unconfirmed or secondhand material to its origin to preserve transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarizing lede of main developments
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a concise summary of the principal factual development (e.g., initial paragraphs saying Allied attacks had broken into Axis positions, or that the 6th Army "has succumbed").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the key fact(s) so readers immediately learn the main outcome or change; follow the lede with supporting detail and chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official communiqués and quoted statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include official statements and quoted material from leaders and governments (examples: communiqués admitting Stalingrad campaign over; quotes from Anthony Eden and Gen. Henri Giraud).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish verbatim or clearly attributed official quotes/communiqués and indicate their source; use them to support claims about strategic developments or morale/political positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete military detail (locations, units, equipment, counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific factual details such as place names, unit types, equipment and numeric counts (e.g., "Two 62-Ton 'Tiger'...88-millimeter guns", "91,000 prisoners", lists of towns captured).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply precise details (town names, unit designations, numbers of casualties, prisoners, tanks, planes, captured materiel) to lend credibility and allow readers to understand scale and geography; where numbers are reported, attribute them if provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyewitness and frontline anecdote inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vivid frontline anecdotes and first-person detail to convey immediacy (examples: "We really got where the shells were thickest", "Scout Car Blown Up", descriptions of tank and air action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate human-scale anecdotes, soldier dialogue, and sensory description to bring events to life; clearly label them as eyewitness or correspondent observation to separate from official claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveating unconfirmed or tentative reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark and qualify unconfirmed or tentative reports (phrases in the text include "Unconfirmed reports say", "Delayed dispatches", references to reconnaissance and 'reportedly').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualifiers (unconfirmed, reported, delayed) when information cannot be independently verified; avoid presenting tentative information as definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing by theatre/section and chronological narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the report into sections by theatre (North Africa, Russia, Caucasus, etc.) and follow a chronological flow within each (e.g., initial action, counterattacks, subsequent developments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the lede, break out coverage by geographic theatre or major thread, and present events in time order so readers can follow sequence and compare fronts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting material captures and damage with totals
rubrics_metrics.description: Report totals for captured or destroyed materiel and damage when available (examples: "750 planes, 1,550 tanks, 90,000 rifles...61,102 trucks"; reports of area razed in Cologne raid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing aggregate numbers of materiel seized/destroyed or damage estimates, present totals clearly and attribute them to an official source or note if they are preliminary; use them to contextualize strategic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of enemy propaganda and opponent statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish significant statements from the enemy side (e.g., German commemorations, Goebbels' orders, German communiqués asserting 'sacrifice not in vain').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report relevant adversary proclamations and propaganda to give readers a fuller picture of morale, official posture, and information warfare; attribute and, if necessary, contextualize such statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evocative, morale-signalling language and ceremonial detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Include ceremonial language and descriptions of mourning or propaganda rituals when newsworthy (examples: martial fanfares, 'Ich Hatt' Einen Kameraden', four days of mourning, closure of entertainment venues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe public ceremonies, morale measures, and cultural signals (funerals, songs, closures) as they reflect the societal impact of military events; note whether such items are official orders or observed practice.
